questions.prompt: In the grains-of-rice doubling story, what kind of function is Snellman introducing?
choices: A A linear function with slope 1.
B An exponential function modeling constant doubling (base b = 2).
C A quadratic with negative discriminant.
D A constant polynomial of degree 0.
questions.explain: Constant doubling illustrates exponential growth; he names the exponential function.

questions.prompt: What restriction does Snellman place on the base b of f(x) = bˣ in his setup?
choices: A b may be any real including 0 and 1 freely.
B Either 0 < b < 1 or b > 1 (excluding 0 and 1).
C Only b = −1.
D Only integer bases greater than 100.
questions.explain: He requires b between 0 and 1 (exclusive) or b > 1—not 0 or 1.

questions.prompt: How does Snellman relate logarithms to inverse functions?
choices: A Logs are unrelated to inverses.
B The log base b is the inverse of the exponential f(x) = bˣ, so log_b(bˣ) = x.
C Logs replace multiplication with exponentiation only.
D Inverse notation f⁻¹ always means 1/f.
questions.explain: He derives log properties from inverse-function behavior: log_b of bˣ returns x.

questions.prompt: What practical algebraic power of logarithms does Snellman stress?
choices: A They force every equation to have no solution.
B Same-base logs can bring exponents “down” so algebra can solve for the variable.
C They convert all functions into linear polynomials automatically.
D They remove the need for a domain.
questions.explain: Logs extract exponents so you can use ordinary algebra on previously exponential unknowns.

questions.prompt: What is the domain of log_b, according to Snellman’s inverse/range argument?
choices: A All real numbers, including negatives and zero.
B (0, ∞)—because the exponential’s range is positive reals, which becomes the log’s domain.
C Only negative integers.
D Exactly {0}.
questions.explain: Range of bˣ is (0, ∞), so that becomes the domain of its inverse, log base b.
